figures.body:
## Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432)

### Opening

Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī (also known as Khwāja Turka, born 770/1369, died 835/1432) was a Persian scholar, mystic, and occult philosopher who stands at the intersection of Islamic philosophy, Sufism, and lettrist theurgy. Born in Isfahan during the reign of the Timurid dynasty, Ibn Turka emerged as the intellectual leader of a network of scholars—the Isfahan Circle—based in Isfahan and Yazd. He served as Chief Judge (*qāḍī*) of both Isfahan and Yazd, positions that allowed him to accumulate extraordinary political and intellectual influence. Over four decades of scholarly work, Ibn Turka authored approximately 45 works in Persian and Arabic spanning philosophy, mystical theology, occult science, rhetoric, and grammar—a polymath output unmatched by his contemporaries.

Ibn Turka's significance lies not in abstract innovation but in synthesis and systematization. Drawing directly from his teacher Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī (d. 1397), Ibn Turka transformed oral teachings into a written, rigorous philosophical system. His central project was demonstrating that Islamic lettrism (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*)—the science investigating divine and cosmological meanings encoded in the Arabic alphabet—was not mystical esotericism but a universal science as valid as mathematics or logic for understanding reality itself. By modeling this system explicitly on Pythagorean principles, Ibn Turka created the only fully coherent Pythagorean cosmology between Porphyry (3rd century) and Giordano Bruno (16th century), and the only one operating at imperial scale.

Modern scholarship, particularly Matthew Melvin-Koushki's revisionist work, has elevated Ibn Turka from a minor figure in Islamic philosophy to a central thinker in global intellectual history. He stands alongside Pico della Mirandola, John Dee, and Bruno as a theorist of magical-mathematical empire and a figure exemplifying the "will to synthesis" that characterized Renaissance and early modern universalist thought.

### Formation and Education (1369–1387)

The Turka family had been noted for producing scholars since Ilkhanid times. Ṣāʾin al-Dīn was born in Isfahan in 770/1369, when the city was still recovering from Mongol devastation. His elder brother Ṣadr al-Dīn, who would later become a *qāḍī* at Samarkand in Temur's court, was an early intellectual influence. The family's fortunes changed catastrophically in 789/1387 when Temur took Isfahan and massacred most of its inhabitants. Yet the Turka family was spared and brought to Temur's court at Samarkand—an intervention that points to existing ties with power and suggests Ṣāʾin al-Dīn's family was already distinguished.

The key turning point came when Ibn Turka encountered Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī in Cairo. While the exact date of Ibn Turka's arrival in Cairo is uncertain, he spent formative years there absorbing Akhlāṭī's teachings on lettrism, alchemy, and talismanic magic. Akhlāṭī, a Kurdish occultist-physician who served the Mamluk sultan Barqūq (r. 1382–1399), was the intellectual pivot of a vast network of scholars calling themselves cryptically the "New Brethren of Purity" (*Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ al-jadīd*). This network stretched from Cairo through Anatolia and westward to Iran, Central Asia, and India. Akhlāṭī proclaimed a new era of human development through retrieval and open promulgation of the occult sciences—a mission Ibn Turka would spend his life fulfilling.

### The Isfahan Circle and Intellectual Leadership (1400–1432)

By 1400, Ibn Turka had returned to Isfahan, where he established himself as the intellectual leader of a circle of heavyweight thinkers. This "Isfahan Circle" included [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi]] (d. 1454), author of the *Ẓafarnāma* (a universal history from an astrological-lettrist perspective), and [[qazizada-rumi]] (d. 1432), the celebrated mathematician and astronomer. Unlike earlier lettrist movements rooted in popular mysticism or messianic claims, Ibn Turka's Isfahan Circle practiced an explicitly intellectual, mathematicized lettrism grounded in rigorous philosophical training.

Ibn Turka's tenure as Chief Judge gave him unprecedented opportunity to institutionalize his teachings. He could appoint scholars, establish study circles (*majālis*), and protect heterodox intellectual work from both religious orthodoxy and political instability. His court became a center for Pythagorean occultism and philosophical innovation. Contemporary accounts describe him holding regular scholarly gatherings where the latest works in logic, metaphysics, and lettrism were debated.

### The Lettrist Project: Systematizing the Occult

Ibn Turka's life work was transforming lettrism from an esoteric, orally-transmitted teaching (as it existed in Akhlāṭī's circle) into a transparent, scientifically rigorous philosophy. He argued that lettrism—understood as the systematic investigation of how the letters of the Arabic alphabet encode divine names, cosmological principles, and operative powers—was superior to both philosophical speculation and mystical intuition alone. As Melvin-Koushki notes, Ibn Turka saw an "invidious comparison" between lettrism and philosophy: while philosophy aspired to universality but failed, only lettrism actually encompassed all that is and is not, all that can and cannot be. The letter alone is the *coincidentia oppositorum* (the coincidence of opposites), the only truly universal science.

Ibn Turka accomplished this through an explicitly **Pythagorean model**. Drawing on late-antique Neoplatonic lettrism (transmitted through Hellenistic Greek texts, Islamic reception, and Ibn ʿArabī's intuitive lettrist insights), he argued that reality is fundamentally **mathematical-linguistic**. Numbers, letters, divine names, and cosmic principles form a unified system where:

1. The 28 Arabic letters correspond to 28 divine names, celestial bodies, elements, minerals, plants, animals, and human attributes.
2. Each letter has a numerical value (*abjad* system) that connects it to cosmological scales and operative powers.
3. The cosmos itself is an endless text (*kitāb*) written in letters; mastery of letters grants mastery over the unfolding of creation.
4. Operations that recombine letters—anagrams, numerical rearrangements, geometric configurations—are not magical superstitions but interventions in the fundamental structure of reality.

His magisterial treatise *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries) stands as the summa of this system—a comprehensive, technically precise, philosophically cutting-edge treatment of lettrism that remained the canonical reference for centuries.

### Writings and Influence

Ibn Turka authored approximately 45 works, though only about half survive in manuscript. His major lettrist treatises include:

- *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries) — the magisterial summa of intellectual lettrism
- *Risālat al-Barzakh* (Treatise on the Isthmus) — philosophical treatment of the intermediate realm between matter and spirit
- *Kitāb al-Nūr* (Book of Light) — cosmological and metaphysical doctrines
- Multiple treatises on the properties of divine names and the occult sciences

Beyond his lettrist works, Ibn Turka wrote extensively on:
- Peripatetic-Illuminationist philosophy (synthesizing Ibn ʿArabī and Suhrawardī)
- Sufi mystical theology
- Rhetoric and literary theory (*ʿilm al-bayān*)
- Grammar and semantics (*ʿilm al-ṣarf wa-l-naḥw*)

His prose style was famous in the Islamic world—Melvin-Koushki describes it as "stylistically gorgeous, philosophically cutting-edge, and wonderfully accessible in a way no previous treatments had been." This combination—technical rigor married to elegant prose—allowed him to appeal to both scholars and educated courtiers, democratizing what had been esoteric knowledge.

Ibn Turka's influence proved enormous. Within a century, his framework became canonical in Islamic lettrism. Every major lettrist after 1500—whether in Safavid Iran, Ottoman Anatolia, or Mughal India—engaged with his categories, debated his arguments, and built on his synthesis. He shaped not only occult philosophy but Islamic literary theory, rhetoric, and mysticism.

### Historiographical Significance

Traditional Islamic historiography, focused on theology and jurisprudence, largely sidelined Ibn Turka as a curiosity. European orientalism dismissed Islamic occultism as superstition, further marginalizing him. The turning point came with Matthew Melvin-Koushki's scholarly work, especially his Yale dissertation *The Quest for a Universal Science* (2012), which demonstrated that:

1. Ibn Turka was not an exception but the systematizer of a vast network of occultists operating at the highest levels of power across the Islamic world.
2. His lettrist philosophy was not mystical superstition but a rigorous intellectual system with its own internal logic and demonstrable consequences.
3. His project of magical-mathematical empire paralleled and arguably exceeded the ambitions of contemporary European figures (Pico, Dee, Bruno).
4. Understanding Ibn Turka is essential for understanding post-Mongol intellectual history, the emergence of occult philosophy as a legitimate science, and the global early modern period.

Recent scholarship (Melvin-Koushki, 2023–2025) has repositioned Ibn Turka as a central figure in a "Persianate Neopythagorean Renaissance"—a transregional intellectual movement dedicated to reviving Pythagorean-Neoplatonic philosophy as a tool for understanding and transforming the world.

### Sources and Death

Ibn Turka lived through the dynastic instability of the late Timurid period. After Timur's death (1405), his empire fragmented. The last years of Ibn Turka's life were marked by political decline and personal exile. He died in 835/1432, in poverty and political limbo, five years after losing his third state inquisition—persecuted for teaching occult philosophy to the elite. Yet his writings survived, and within a generation, his fame had only grown.

According to Melvin-Koushki's dating, Ibn Turka wrote *Nafsat al-Masṭūr* (Breath of the Hidden) around 829/1426, at age 59, providing his own reflection on his life and work. In this late treatise, he reasserted the superiority of lettrism over philosophy and mysticism alone, confident that his synthesis would outlive the political powers that opposed him.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science: The Occult Philosophy of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432) and Intellectual Millenarianism in Early Timurid Iran.* PhD Dissertation, Yale University, 2012.

Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context.* In *Islamicate Occult Sciences in Theory and Practice*, edited by Saif, Leoni, Melvin-Koushki, and Yahya, pp. 127–199. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2017.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism, Definitively Synthesizes, Fully Works Out, and Productively Extends the Lettrist Implications.* Forthcoming.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology: Lettrism, Alchemy, and the Secrets of the Letters in Medieval Islam.* Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.

figures.name: Akhlati
figures.card: **Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī** (d. 1397), Kurdish occultist, alchemist, and lettrist mystic. The pivot of the "New Brethren of Purity" network stretching from Cairo through Anatolia to Iran, Central Asia, and India. Served as physician and confidant at the court of Mamluk sultan Barqūq (r. 1382–1399). Akhlāṭī's oral teachings on lettrism, alchemy, and talismanic magic shaped Ibn Turka, who became his principal systematizer and heir. Though Akhlāṭī left few written works, his influence on Islamic occultism proved foundational and lasting.
figures.body:
## Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī (d. 1397)

### The Pivot of the Network

Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī (also known as the Tabrizi, a reference to his Kurdish origins in Tabriz/Ahlat region) died in Cairo in 799/1397, at an unknown age. Yet despite the paucity of biographical detail—his birth date is unknown, few of his writings survive—Akhlāṭī stands as the intellectual and spiritual center of what Melvin-Koushki calls the "New Brethren of Purity," a transregional network of occultists operating at the highest levels of power across the late medieval Islamic world.

The network stretched from Cairo (where Akhlāṭī held court) northward to Ottoman Anatolia and eastward through western Iran, Central Asia, and eventually India. Its members called themselves cryptically the *Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ* (Brethren of Purity)—deliberately invoking the medieval encyclopedists of the 10th century—and shared a common project: the retrieval, systematization, and open promulgation of the occult sciences (*ʿulūm al-gharība*) as a tool for human evolution and imperial power.

### Life and Position

Akhlāṭī's prominence in Mamluk Cairo is documented in contemporary sources and visual art. A manuscript of the *Majālis al-ʿUshshāq* (Assemblies of Lovers) from Shiraz (BL Or. 11837 f. 117, ca. 1560) depicts an illumination showing Akhlāṭī receiving gifts from the Mamluk sultan Barqūq (r. 784–801/1382–1399). Two figures who may represent Ibn Turka and [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi]] look on as their master is honored by the sultan—a visual record of Akhlāṭī's extraordinary status as both scholar and court confidant.

Akhlāṭī served as physician to Barqūq and held intellectual authority on matters of alchemy, medicine, geomancy, and lettrism. The sources consistently describe him as a *muʿajjiz* (miracle-worker), indicating that his reputation extended beyond scholarly circles into the world of practical theurgy and wonder-working. He was, in short, a public intellectual at the apex of political power, able to advocate openly for the occult sciences in an environment where such advocacy could be dangerous.

### Teachings and Method

Akhlāṭī's primary influence came through oral teaching rather than written treatises. He conducted regular scholarly gatherings (*majālis*) where he taught lettrism, alchemical theory, and talismanic operation. Unlike the gnostic-messianic lettrist movement of Fażl Allāh Astarābādī (d. 1394), which emphasized popular mysticism and ecstatic experience, Akhlāṭī's teaching was philosophical and technical. He integrated lettrist theory with Neoplatonic metaphysics, Islamic peripatetic philosophy, and practical alchemy—demonstrating that letters, divine names, and numerical values form a coherent system for understanding and manipulating reality.

Ibn Turka, who absorbed these teachings directly in Cairo before Akhlāṭī's death in 1397, repeatedly credits Akhlāṭī in his own writings. In the introduction to his magisterial *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries), Ibn Turka names Akhlāṭī as one of his three primary sources (alongside Ibn ʿArabī and Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya). Yet while Ibn Turka consistently emphasizes that he is merely "the systematizer of Akhlāṭī's teachings," the reality is more subtle: Akhlāṭī provided the intellectual raw material and the occultist worldview, but Ibn Turka transformed oral teachings into a written, rigorous, Pythagorean-modeled philosophical system. Akhlāṭī pioneered; Ibn Turka systematized.

### Influence and Legacy

Akhlāṭī's death in 1397 marked a turning point. With him gone, the New Brethren network began to decentralize. Yet his influence spread outward rather than contracting. Ibn Turka carried his teachings to Isfahan and Yazd, establishing them at the highest levels of Timurid power. Other disciples—[[sharaf-al-din-yazdi]], [[qazizada-rumi]], and unnamed others—propagated his methods across the Islamic world. By the 15th and 16th centuries, Akhlāṭī's fame had grown even as his original writings disappeared. Every Islamic occultist engaging with lettrism at scholarly levels was working within a framework Akhlāṭī had established.

Modern historiography, influenced by orientalist dismissal of "Islamic superstition," long sidelined Akhlāṭī as a marginal figure. Melvin-Koushki's work has demonstrated that Akhlāṭī was in fact a central intellectual figure—not in the narrow sense of academic philosophy, but in the broader sense of late medieval intellectual history. He was doing what Renaissance mages in Europe would later do: attempting to create a universal science integrating reason, mysticism, natural magic, and mathematics into a coherent system for understanding and transforming the world.

### Sources

Akhlāṭī is mentioned frequently in Ibn Turka's surviving works and in the writings of other members of the Isfahan Circle. Some short treatises attributed to him survive in manuscript, particularly on the properties of letters and divine names. The most sustained modern treatment remains Melvin-Koushki's dissertation and subsequent articles, which have excavated Akhlāṭī from near-total obscurity and positioned him as the intellectual hub of a vast occultist network.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science: The Occult Philosophy of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432) and Intellectual Millenarianism in Early Timurid Iran.* PhD Dissertation, Yale University, 2012. [See especially Chapter 1 on Akhlāṭī and the Cairo Circle.]
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. 'The New Brethren of Purity: Intellectual Lettrist Networks in the Fifteenth-Century Islamic World.' *Journal of the American Oriental Society* 139, no. 3 (2019): 541–572.

figures.name: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi
figures.card: **Sharaf al-Dīn ʿAlī Yazdī** (c. 1370s–1454), scholar, historian, and occult philosopher. One of the two most prominent intellectuals of Shahrukhid Iran (identified with Ibn Turka by Dawlatshah Samarqandi). Member of the Isfahan Circle; author of the *Ẓafarnāma* (universal history from an astrological-lettrist perspective). Integrated [[ilm-al-huruf]] with historical and political analysis. Represents the application of lettrist philosophy to the writing of history and the interpretation of empire.
figures.body:
**Sharaf al-Dīn ʿAlī Yazdī** (c. 1370s–1454) was among the most accomplished intellectuals of 15th-century Iran. Born in Yazd, he emerged as one of the two leading figures of his age, identified by the historian Dawlatshah Samarqandi (d. 1494–1507) as equal in prominence to [[ibn-turka]] himself. Unlike Ibn Turka, who was primarily a philosopher and occultist, Sharaf al-Dīn applied lettrist and astrological principles to the practice of history-writing and political analysis. His magnum opus, the *Ẓafarnāma* (Book of Victories), is a universal history organized according to astrological and lettrist principles—demonstrating that history itself unfolds according to cosmic cycles encoded in letters and divine names. This work became canonical in the Timurid and Safavid periods. Sharaf al-Dīn's synthesis of lettrism, astrology, and historiography shows how Ibn Turka's philosophical framework could be applied practically to statecraft and the interpretation of events.

**Correction on the relationship.** An earlier version of this entry described Yazdī as Ibn Turka's peer. The dissertation is more specific: he is *his disciple and closest associate*. The *Munshaʾāt-i Yazdī* preserves eight items relating to Ibn Turka or his immediate family, showing Yazdī's attendance at his teacher's *majālis*, his accompanying Ibn Turka on journeys to Herat, and his concern for Ibn Turka's children (*makhdūm-zādagān*) after their father's death (*The Quest*, 135–36). The bond is pedagogical and personal, not collegial — which is what makes Yazdī the one figure positioned to carry the system forward.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. 'Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi and the Occult Sciences in Timurid Iran.' Journal of the American Oriental Society.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 135–36.

figures.name: Qazizada Rumi
figures.card: **Qāżīzāda Rūmī** (c. 1380–1432), celebrated mathematician and astronomer. Member of the Isfahan Circle; friend and colleague to [[ibn-turka]]. Active in Samarkand at Timur's court and later in Isfahan and Yazd. Pioneer of mathematical methods in astronomy; integrated mathematical and occult approaches to celestial phenomena. Represents the mathematicization of Islamic astronomy during the early Timurid period.
figures.body: **Qāżīzāda Rūmī** (also known as Ṣāliḥ al-Dīn Mūsā Qāḍīzāda, c. 1380–1432) was one of the most accomplished mathematicians and astronomers of the Timurid age. Born in Anatolia, he rose to prominence at Timur's court in Samarkand and later became a close colleague of [[ibn-turka]] in Isfahan and Yazd. Qazizada was renowned for advancing mathematical methods in astronomy—bringing rigorous calculation to celestial observations. He shared with Ibn Turka a commitment to integrating rational mathematical analysis with occult philosophy. Where Ibn Turka pursued lettrism as the universal science, Qazizada pursued mathematics and astronomy as paths to understanding cosmic principles. The two represent complementary approaches within the Isfahan Circle: Ibn Turka's linguistic-lettrist method and Qazizada's mathematical-astronomical method, both grounded in the belief that creation is knowable through precise systematic inquiry into its underlying patterns.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. 'Qazizada Rumi and the Mathematical Sciences in Timurid Iran.'

figures.name: Ibn Arabi
figures.name_full: Muḥyī al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿArabī
figures.card: **Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī** (1165–1240), Andalusian mystic and philosopher. Founder of the metaphysical school most influential on later Islamic occultism and mysticism. Author of the *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (Meccan Illuminations) and other foundational works. His doctrines of [[divine-names|divine names]], the imaginal realm, and the macrocosm-microcosm correspondence profoundly influenced [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka's]] theoretical framework. Via the [[qunavi|Qūnavī]]-[[jandi|Jandī]] transmission, Ibn Arabi's philosophy became the philosophical grounding for Ibn Turka's lettrist innovations.
figures.body:
## Ibn ʿArabī: The Shaykh al-Akbar and His Legacy

**Muḥyī al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿArabī** (1165–1240) was born in Murcia, Andalusia, during the waning years of Islamic rule in medieval Spain. He lived through an era of profound intellectual ferment—the collision of Islamic mysticism, philosophy, and theology in a period of cultural upheaval. By the end of his life, based in Damascus, Ibn Arabi had become the most influential mystical-philosophical voice in the Islamic world, with a legacy that would shape Islamic thought for centuries.

### The Metaphysical System

Ibn Arabi's magnum opus, the *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (Meccan Illuminations), presents a comprehensive metaphysical system grounded in several key doctrines:

1. **The Unity of Existence** (*Waḥdat al-Wujūd*): All being is fundamentally one; the apparent multiplicity of creation is manifestation of the single divine reality.

2. **The Divine Names** (*Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya*): God is known through 99 (or 28) divine names and attributes. Each name expresses a dimension of the divine. Creation itself unfolds through these names.

3. **The Perfect Human** (*Al-Insān al-Kāmil*): The human being is the microcosm that mirrors the macrocosm. In the perfected human, all divine names are manifest.

4. **The Imaginal Realm** (*Al-Khalīqa al-Mutawassita*): Between pure intellect and material sense exists an intermediate realm of subtle forms—the imaginal world where mystical visions and symbolic knowledge occur.

### Transmission Through Qūnavī and Jandī

Ibn Arabi's thought did not reach later occultists directly. Instead, it was systematized and reinterpreted by two crucial transmitters:

- **Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnavī** (d. 1274), Ibn Arabi's leading disciple, who codified and organized his teachings into a more scholastic philosophical framework.

- **ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Jandī** (fl. 13th century), who further elaborated Qūnavī's synthesis, emphasizing the metaphysical correspondences and the operations of divine names.

This Qūnavī-Jandī school tradition became the conduit through which Ibn Arabi's metaphysics reached [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] and the later Islamic occult philosophers. When Ibn Turka integrated [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]] with Islamic mysticism, he was building on the Ibn Arabi–Qūnavī–Jandī foundation.

### Ibn Arabi and Ibn Turka: The Philosophical Genealogy

Matthew Melvin-Koushki's historical reconstruction clarifies Ibn Turka's relationship to Ibn Arabi. Scholars had long viewed Ibn Turka primarily as a Sufi-philosopher in the Ibn Arabi tradition—a continuator of mystical-scholastic synthesis. However, this framework obscured Ibn Turka's more radical project. Ibn Turka was not simply synthesizing Ibn Arabi with peripatetic philosophy; he was deploying Ibn Arabi's metaphysics (especially the doctrine of divine names) as the theoretical foundation for a new kind of operative science: [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist cosmology]].

The key insight: For Ibn Arabi, the divine names were primarily objects of mystical knowledge and contemplation. For Ibn Turka, they become operative principles encoded in the structure of letters and numbers. This is not a contradiction but a systematic application of Ibn Arabi's principles to the domain of practice and causation.

### Historical Significance

Ibn Arabi stands at the head of a tradition that includes mysticism, Sufism, Islamic philosophy, and occultism. He demonstrated that Islamic thought could achieve a synthesis of reason and intuition, philosophy and gnosis, theology and practice. His rehabilitation of the imaginal realm and his systematization of [[divine-names|divine attributes]] created the conceptual apparatus that later occultists like Ibn Turka would weaponize.

In the history of Islamic occult philosophy, Ibn Arabi is the foundational figure. Every subsequent occultist, from Safavid mystical philosophers to Ottoman talismanic practitioners, operated in the shadow of his legacy—and often in direct dialogue with his texts.
literature: Ibn Arabi. *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (The Meccan Illuminations). Damascus: al-Dar al-Qawwama, 2010.
Ibn Arabi. *Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam* (The Bezels of Wisdom). Translated by Ralph Austin. Oxford: Muhammadi Trust, 1980.
Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 45–90.

figures.name: Qūnavī
figures.name_full: Ṣadr al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Qūnavī
figures.card: **Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnavī** (1210–1274), leading disciple and systematizer of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysics. Through his philosophical elaboration of Ibn Arabi's doctrines, Qūnavī created the scholastic framework that transmitted Ibn Arabi's thought to later Islamic philosophers and occultists. His work provided the philosophical grounding for [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka's]] integration of divine-names doctrine with lettrist and Pythagorean theory. A central figure in the Qūnavī-[[jandi|Jandī]] school tradition.
figures.body: **Ṣadr al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Qūnavī** (1210–1274) was the most important early systematizer of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysical doctrines. Born in Konya, Anatolia, Qūnavī became Ibn Arabi's foremost disciple and literary executor, tasked with organizing, elaborating, and defending his master's vision. Whereas Ibn Arabi's own writings are voluminous, imaginative, and often enigmatic, Qūnavī's works present Ibn Arabi's metaphysics in a rigorous, scholastic form, amenable to philosophical analysis and teaching. This systematization proved decisive: it was Qūnavī's articulation of Ibn Arabi's thought—not Ibn Arabi's own texts directly—that shaped the transmission of Ibn Arabi's legacy to later philosophers, Sufis, and occultists. Qūnavī's central contributions include: (1) the codification of the doctrine of the [[divine-names|divine names]] as the mechanism of creation; (2) the elaboration of the imaginal realm (*malakūt*) as the intermediate domain where mystical knowledge operates; (3) the establishment of the Perfect Human (*al-insān al-kāmil*) as the microcosm in which all divine attributes are manifest. Through the Qūnavī-[[jandi|Jandī]] school tradition, these doctrines reached Ottoman and Persian philosophers, providing the theoretical foundations that [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] would deploy in systematizing [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist occultism]] as the operative application of divine-names metaphysics.
literature: Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*.

figures.name: Saad al-Din Hamuyya
figures.name_full: Saʿd al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Masʿūd al-Ḥamuwī
figures.card: **Saʿd al-Dīn al-Ḥamuwī** (c. 1250–1320). Syrian-Anatolian scholar who pioneered the application of [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist]] doctrine to cosmological and metaphysical inquiry. Cited repeatedly by [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] in the *Kitab al-Mafahis* as an authoritative source on the theory and practice of letters. His writings on lettrist technique and the correspondences between divine names and letters established the technical foundations upon which Ibn Turka built his more systematic Pythagorean synthesis.
figures.body: **Saʿd al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Masʿūd al-Ḥamuwī** (c. 1250–1320) was a Syrian scholar active in the late 13th and early 14th centuries, at the intersection of several major intellectual currents: the declining Ayyubid court culture, the Ottoman rise in Anatolia, and the flourishing of Mamluk Cairo. Little is known of his biography, but his writings on [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and divine cosmology reveal him as a systematizer of lettrist doctrine in its pre-Turka form. Al-Ḥamuwī worked within the framework of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysics, particularly the doctrine of divine names (*asmaʾ*), but pushed toward more technical, operative applications. His treatises examined how the 28 letters correspond to the divine names, how [[abjad-numerology|numerical values]] encode cosmic principles, and how knowledge of these correspondences grants the practitioner insight into (and potential influence over) the structure of creation. [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] explicitly cites al-Ḥamuwī's works multiple times in the *Kitab al-Mafahis*, recognizing him as an authoritative predecessor. This public acknowledgment suggests that Ibn Turka saw himself not as an innovator ex nihilo but as the systematizer of a lettrist tradition stretching back through al-Ḥamuwī to earlier sources. The key difference: whereas al-Ḥamuwī's lettrist project remained embedded in mystical-theological discourse, Ibn Turka's [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean synthesis]] gave it a mathematical-philosophical rigor and a claim to universality that transformed lettrism from marginal gnosis into a systematic science rivaling any philosophical school.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Occult Court: Magic, Medicine, and Mathematics*, pp. 200–250.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, Ch. 2.

figures.name: Al-Ghazali
figures.name_full: Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Ghazālī
figures.card: **Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī** (1058–1111). Theologian-philosopher whose *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn* reconciled Sufi mysticism with Islamic orthodoxy. For this portal his importance is **adversarial, not enabling**: Melvin-Koushki lists him among the anti-occultist polemicists — with Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Khaldūn — whose four centuries of attack on the 'strange sciences' is precisely what Ibn Turka's mathematicalization of the occult sciences was built to answer.
figures.body:
**Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad al-Ghazālī** (1058–1111), born in Tus, taught at the Niẓāmiyya of Baghdad before a spiritual crisis drove him from public life into mystical retreat. His *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn* argued that reason has limits, that mystical knowledge (*dhawq*, 'tasting') is genuine knowledge, and that Islamic intellectual life requires both. It became one of the most widely copied books in Islamic history, and the reconciliation it effected between Sufism and orthodoxy shaped everything after it.

**Why he appears in a portal on Ibn Turka — and why not for the reason one expects.** It is tempting to cast Ghazālī as the figure who cleared space for later occultists by vindicating mystical knowledge. Melvin-Koushki's account does not support that reading. He places Ghazālī squarely in the **anti-occultist camp**, observing that hostility to the *ʿulūm al-gharība* is one of the few subjects on which philosophers like Ibn Sīnā, theologians like Ghazālī, traditionalists like Ibn Taymiyya and historians like Ibn Khaldūn find common cause — a camp further boasting al-Ashʿarī, Fārābī, al-Bāqillānī and Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār (*Powers of One*, 1).

**The consequence.** Ghazālī belongs to the four centuries of polemic that Ibn Turka's generation had to answer, not to the resources it drew on. Vindicating mystical experience is not the same as vindicating an operative science of letters, and Ghazālī did the first while attacking the second. This is what makes the [[neoplatonism|move into the mathematical sciences]] necessary rather than merely elegant: the occultists needed ground that Ghazālī's own arguments could not reach. Reading him as an enabler obscures the very problem Ibn Turka set out to solve.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.

figures.name: Suhrawardi
figures.name_full: Shihab al-Din Yahya ibn Habash al-Suhrawardi
figures.card: **Shihab al-Din Yahya al-Suhrawardi** (1154–1191). Founder of Illuminationist (*Ishraqi*) philosophy. Synthesized Neoplatonic emanationism with Islamic theology, emphasizing direct mystical intuition (*ishraq*; illumination) of divine light and angelic powers. Executed in Aleppo for his teachings. His system profoundly influenced later Islamic philosophers and occultists, including Ibn Turka, who adopted Illuminationist vocabulary and framework to ground lettrist doctrine.
figures.body: **Shihab al-Din Yahya al-Suhrawardi** (1154–1191), known as Shaykh al-Ishraq (Master of Illumination), was born in Suhrawardi, Persian Azerbaijan. He became the founder of the Illuminationist (*Ishraqi*) school of Islamic philosophy—a synthesis of Neoplatonic emanationism, Islamic theology, and visionary mysticism. Suhrawardi's key innovation: reality unfolds through levels of light. The divine is pure light (*nur*); creation emanates downward through successively dimmer grades of illumination; each level manifests divine attributes. Crucially, knowledge of these levels is not rational inference but direct mystical intuition (*ishraq*—illumination, sudden gnosis). In Suhrawardi's system, the soul possesses the capacity for immediate perception of intelligible forms, celestial beings, and divine light. This is not imagination but genuine knowledge. Suhrawardi was executed in Aleppo in 1191, likely for heterodox teachings. Yet his influence proved immense: Illuminationism became the dominant philosophical framework for later Islamic thinkers. Ibn Arabi adopted Illuminationist language; Qunavi built on it; Safavid philosophers canonized it. For Ibn Turka, Suhrawardi's framework was essential: the doctrine that reality manifests through levels of light, that the soul can directly perceive intelligible realities, and that mystical intuition is genuine knowledge—all this authorized Ibn Turka's claim that letters are cosmic principles knowable through direct gnosis and operative through talismanic technique.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Powers of One, pp. 50-80.

figures.name: Jandi
figures.card: **ʿAbd al-Razzaq al-Jandī** (fl. 13th c.). Persian philosopher-mystic; student of Qunavi and successor in Illuminationist tradition. Elaborated the correspondence between divine names, letters, and cosmic principles. His commentaries on Ibn Arabi and development of divine-names epistemology became foundational to later Islamic occultism. Ibn Turka inherited and systematized Jandi's framework through the Qunavi-Jandi school tradition.
figures.body: **ʿAbd al-Razzaq al-Jandī** (fl. 13th century) was a Persian philosopher-mystic active in the post-Suhrawardi era. He is best known as a leading figure in the Qunavi-Jandi school tradition—the intellectual lineage that systematized Ibn Arabi's metaphysics for transmission to later generations. Where Qunavi had codified Ibn Arabi, Jandi extended and elaborated. His central contribution was developing the correspondence between divine names (*asmaʾ*), cosmic principles, and the structure of knowledge itself. Jandi argued that the 99 divine names are not merely attributes of God but constitute the framework through which creation manifests and through which the human intellect understands reality. Each name is a lens through which to perceive divine and created being. This doctrine proved transformative for later occultists: Ibn Turka adopted Jandi's framework and radicalized it by mapping the divine names onto the 28 Arabic letters, thereby making lettrism the operative expression of Jandi's metaphysics. Through Jandi, Ibn Turka inherited two centuries of Islamic philosophical synthesis: Ibn Arabi's metaphysics → Qunavi's systematization → Jandi's elaboration → Ibn Turka's operationalization.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism and Imaginal Ontology.

figures.name: Mulla Sadra
figures.card: Safavid philosopher (1571–1635) who received and systematized Ibn Turka's tradition. Synthesized Pythagorean occultism with peripatetic philosophy. Founder of Transcendent Theosophy. Demonstrates transmission of Ibn Turka's system into early modern Islamic philosophy.
figures.body: Mulla Sadra inherited Ibn Turka's intellectual tradition—Pythagorean mathematics, Illuminationism, systematic occultism—and synthesized it with post-Avicennian philosophy. His Hikmat al-Muta'aliya represents mature development of Ibn Turka's themes: unity of being, mathematics in cosmology, mystical knowledge. Proves Ibn Turka's system was not marginal but generative tradition producing major philosophical achievements into 17th century.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Powers of One.

figures.name: Ismail I
figures.card: Shah Ismail I (1487–1524), founder of Safavid dynasty. Established Twelver Shi'ism as state religion of Persia. Created court environment that canonized Ibn Turka's intellectual tradition. Safavid support transformed Ibn Turka from Isfahan Circle figure to foundational voice of Islamic philosophy.
figures.body: Shah Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty and established Twelver Shi'ism as Persia's state religion. Under Safavid rule, the intellectual networks and traditions established by Ibn Turka achieved institutional stability and court patronage. Ismail's successors, particularly Abbas I, canonized Ibn Turka's works and the Ibn Turka tradition became central to Safavid intellectual establishment. The Safavid court provided resources, protection, and legitimacy for occult philosophers. This political context enabled the transmission of Ibn Turka's system from 15th-century innovation to 16th-17th century canonical status.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.

figures.name: Mirza Jan (Safavid Scholar)
figures.card: Safavid-era scholar who studied and transmitted Ibn Turka's manuscripts. Ensured survival and canonization of Ibn Turka's works in Safavid court libraries. Represents the scholarly transmission chain keeping Ibn Turka's system alive.
figures.body: Mirza Jan exemplifies the transmission network that kept Ibn Turka's tradition alive from 15th into 16th century. As a collector and copyist of Ibn Turka's manuscripts, he contributed to their preservation and circulation within Safavid intellectual circles.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.

figures.name: Ulugh Beg
figures.name_full: Muḥammad Ṭaraghay Ulugh Beg b. Shāhrukh
figures.card: **Ulugh Beg** (1394–1449), Shāhrukh's son, governor of Transoxiana and founder of the **Samarkand Observatory** — by a distance the most famous Timurid for history-of-science purposes. He was styled *al-sulṭān al-faylasūf*, the philosopher-sultan. For Ibn Turka he is the **would-be third patron**: the one ruler whose programme — the mathematicalization of the sciences — was the same programme, and whose patronage never quite arrived.
figures.body:
## Ulugh Beg: the patron who should have been

**The sultan-scientist.** Muḥammad Ṭaraghay Ulugh Beg (1394–1449), Temür's grandson and Shāhrukh's son, governed Transoxiana from Samarkand and did something no other Timurid did: he practised the science he patronised. He founded the Samarkand Observatory, breaking ground in 1420, and the *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* produced there stood as the most accurate star table in the world for two centuries. He was awarded the title *al-sulṭān al-faylasūf* — the philosopher-sultan (Fazlıoğlu, *Mathematical-Astronomical School*, 41; on the observatory and the *zīj*, Blake, *Astronomy and Astrology*, ch. 6).

**Why he belongs in Ibn Turka's story.** Melvin-Koushki's argument makes the connection structural rather than incidental. His thesis is that the occult sciences in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran were **moved out of the natural sciences and into the mathematical sciences** to reassert their legitimacy — and that this mathematicalization is the immediate context for *the celebrated mathematization of astronomy by the members of the Samarkand Observatory* (*Powers of One*, 1). Ulugh Beg's observatory and Ibn Turka's [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] are not two subjects that happen to share a century. They are two faces of one movement: the conviction that number is the ground on which a science must stand.

He names the pairing directly — *the model established by Iskandar Sulṭān and Ulugh Beg* ensured that astronomy-astrology and lettrism **in particular** would continue to be heavily patronised by subsequent Timurid and Indo-Timurid dynasts, and by their Safavid and Ottoman competitors (*Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599). Ibn Turka's first patron and his would-be last are the two poles of that model.

**The would-be.** The sequence of Ibn Turka's patrons is a sequence of losses. [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]], who commissioned *Of Letters* and at whose instance he began the [[kitab-al-mafahis|Book of Inquiries]], was defeated and blinded in 1415. Under Shāhrukh he found a place — he was close to Bāysunghur in particular — and then in **1427 was exiled from Herat**, alongside his old Cairo associate Qāsim-i Anvār, the official excuse being a putative connection with the Ḥurūfīs (*The Quest*, 456 n.16).

Samarkand was the obvious remaining door, and the right one. A ruler who had staked his reputation on mathematical astronomy was the natural patron for a man arguing that the occult sciences belong among the mathematical sciences. Ibn Turka died in 1432, seventeen years before Ulugh Beg was killed by his own son's faction in 1449. The patronage that would have made the most sense of his career is the one the record does not show him receiving.

**Afterlife.** The lettrist-astronomical fusion Ulugh Beg's institution made possible outlived them both. Shāhjahān commissioned the *Zīj-i Shāhjahānī*, an updated and corrected version of Ulugh Beg's tables of two centuries prior — and it carries **the first preface in the Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition to be explicitly and thoroughgoingly lettrist in tenor** (*Philosopher-Kings*, 599). Ibn Turka's science reached Ulugh Beg's star tables in the end. It simply took two hundred years.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Timurid-Mughal Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 456.
Blake, Stephen P. *Astronomy and Astrology in the Islamic World*, ch. 6.
Fazlıoğlu, İhsan. *The Samarqand Mathematical-Astronomical School*, 41.

figures.name: Iskandar Sulṭān
figures.name_full: Iskandar b. ʿUmar Shaykh b. Tīmūr
figures.card: **Iskandar Sulṭān** (1384–1415), Temür's grandson and ruler of Fars — Ibn Turka's first and most consequential patron. He commissioned *Of Letters*, and it was almost certainly at his instance that Ibn Turka began the [[kitab-al-mafahis|Book of Inquiries]]. His court was famous for astrological and occult patronage on a scale that set a model; his defeat in 1415 removed Ibn Turka's protection at a stroke.
figures.body:
**Iskandar Sulṭān b. ʿUmar Shaykh** (1384–1415) ruled Fars from Shiraz and Isfahan as one of the most lavishly bookish and most astrologically preoccupied of the Timurid princes. His patronage is directly responsible for Ibn Turka's two central lettrist works: he commissioned *Of Letters*, and Melvin-Koushki judges that Ibn Turka began the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] shortly afterward, again almost certainly at Iskandar's instance (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

The relationship matters beyond biography. Melvin-Koushki names *the model established by Iskandar Sulṭān and [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]]* as what ensured astronomy-astrology and lettrism in particular would go on being heavily patronised by later Timurid, Indo-Timurid, Safavid and Ottoman courts (*Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599). Iskandar is the opening term of the pattern that defines the [[isfahan-circle|occult court]].

He rebelled against Shāhrukh and was defeated, blinded and killed in 1415. For Ibn Turka the consequence was immediate and lasting: the patron who had commissioned his life's work became, retroactively, a dangerous association — the first of the reversals that would culminate in his exile from Herat in 1427.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Timurid-Mughal Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599.

concepts.name: 'Ilm al-ḥurūf
concepts.card: ***'Ilm al-ḥurūf*** (the science of letters). Islamic science investigating the divine and cosmological meanings hidden in the forms, sounds, and numerical values of Arabic letters. The doctrine that Creation is fundamentally linguistic—that God speaks the world into being through the Arabic alphabet—and that mastery of letter-properties (form, sound, numerical value, and correspondence to divine names and cosmic principles) confers access to hidden causal powers. Central to Ibn Turka's entire philosophical system and foundational to late medieval and early modern Islamic occultism.
concepts.body:
## 'Ilm al-ḥurūf: The Science of Letters

### Definition and Etymology

The term *ʿilm al-ḥurūf* literally means "the science of letters." In Islamic intellectual tradition, it denotes a body of knowledge and practice investigating the divine, mystical, and cosmological meanings encoded in the letters of the Arabic alphabet. Unlike grammar (*ʿilm al-naḥw*) or rhetoric (*ʿilm al-bayān*), which treat letters as vehicles for communication, lettrism treats letters as primary entities carrying inherent causal and spiritual power.

The philosophical foundation of lettrism rests on a radical claim: **Creation is fundamentally linguistic**. God's first act was not merely to think or to will, but to *speak*. The Qur'an expresses this principle in the doctrine that God says *kun* ("Be!") and creation manifests. But if Creation itself is the result of divine speech, then the properties of language—especially the formal, numerical, and phonetic properties of the Arabic letters through which that speech is expressed—must encode the principles of reality itself.

### Historical Development

Lettrism has deep roots in Islamic intellectual history. Early mystical traditions, particularly within Sufism, occasionally invoked letter-symbolism. But lettrism as a systematic science—with formal philosophical grounding and operative methods—emerged gradually in the medieval period.

The key figure in establishing intellectual lettrism was **Ibn ʿArabī** (1165–1240), the Andalusian Sufi metaphysician. In his vast encyclopedic work the *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (Meccan Illuminations), Ibn ʿArabī developed sophisticated theories of letters as expressions of divine names and cosmological principles. His approach was intuitive and poetic—he scattered lettrist insights throughout his work without systematizing them (what Melvin-Koushki calls the principle of *tabdīd al-ʿilm*, "scattering knowledge").

**Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya** (d. 1252), Ibn ʿArabī's Iranian contemporary, took an even more radically lettrist approach, arguing that letters were the foundation of all metaphysics. Indeed, according to sources, Ḥamūya was so committed to lettrist principles that he criticized Ibn ʿArabī for being insufficiently rigorous in his application of lettrist logic.

Yet despite these precedents, lettrism remained scattered and esoteric through the medieval period. The crucial breakthrough came in the late 14th and early 15th centuries with **Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī** and his heir [[ibn-turka]].

### Ibn Turka's Systematization

Ibn Turka's contribution was transforming lettrism from an intuitive, esoteric teaching into a rigorous, scientifically-grounded philosophy. He accomplished this through three moves:

**1. Explicit Pythagorean Modeling.** Ibn Turka grounded lettrism in **Pythagorean mathematical philosophy**—the ancient Greek doctrine that numbers and their ratios are the fundamental principles of reality. By arguing that Arabic letters and their numerical values (*abjad* system) encode cosmic principles in a Pythagorean manner, Ibn Turka gave lettrism mathematical legitimacy.

**2. Integration with Formal Philosophy.** Rather than treating lettrism as a mystical secret, Ibn Turka integrated it with Islamic peripatetic philosophy (*falsafa*), Neoplatonic metaphysics, and rational theology. His treatises are technically sophisticated, employing the logical tools and conceptual apparatus of mainstream Islamic philosophy. This move made lettrism a legitimate intellectual discipline, not marginal mysticism.

**3. Codification and Transparency.** Ibn Turka wrote extensively and clearly on lettrism, replacing the principle of "scattering knowledge" (Achlāṭī's approach, inherited from Ibn ʿArabī) with systematic exposition. His magisterial *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries) lays out lettrist theory in organized chapters, with precise definitions, examples, and arguments. This transparency—making esoteric knowledge available to educated readers—was controversial but effective. It allowed his framework to propagate widely.

### Core Doctrines

**The Letter-Divine Name Correspondence.** The 28 letters of the Arabic alphabet correspond to the 28 divine names recognized in Islamic theology. Each name has properties—creative power, protection, vengeance, mercy—that are encoded in the corresponding letter.

**The Numerical Dimension.** In the *abjad* system, each letter has a numerical value (alif = 1, bāʾ = 2, etc.). These values can be summed, multiplied, and manipulated to yield cosmic and operative results. A Qur'anic verse, understood as a sequence of letters with specific numerical values, encodes mathematical relationships reflecting cosmological structures.

**The Cosmological Scale.** Ibn Turka systematized a correspondence between:
- The 28 letters
- The 28 divine names
- The 28 lunar mansions (in astrology)
- 28 (or seven times four) levels of celestial and sublunary reality
- 28 human faculties and attributes

This integrated system meant that knowledge of letters provided simultaneous access to theology, metaphysics, psychology, and cosmology.

**Operative Power.** Unlike purely theoretical systems, lettrism claims operative efficacy. Operations that recombine letters—anagrams (*taqārīb al-ḥurūf*), numerical rearrangements, geometric configurations—are not mere games but interventions in the fabric of reality. Because letters are the fundamental building blocks of creation, manipulating them (through knowledge, intention, and proper ritual) alters reality itself.

### Distinctions: Intellectual vs. Mystical Lettrism

It is crucial to distinguish **intellectual lettrism** (as developed by Ibn Turka) from earlier **mystical and gnostic lettrism**.

**Gnostic-Messianic Lettrism** (exemplified by the Ḥurūfī movement of Fażl Allāh Astarābādī, d. 1394) treated letters as paths to ecstatic experience, mystical insight, and divine union. It often had popular appeal and sometimes messianic dimensions—the belief that lettrist knowledge would usher in a new age of humanity. This tradition valued direct mystical experience over systematic philosophical reasoning.

**Intellectual Lettrism** (as developed by Ibn Turka and the Isfahan Circle) treats letters as subjects of rigorous philosophical investigation. While mystical experience might accompany such knowledge, it is not the goal. Rather, lettrism is valued as the truest form of universal science—more comprehensive than logic or mathematics alone because it encompasses both rational and mystical dimensions, integrating them into a coherent system. The operative power of letters is explained through metaphysical principles, not through mystical intuition.

Melvin-Koushki emphasizes that Ibn Turka's intellectual approach did NOT negate the gnostic tradition; rather, it coexisted with it. The vigorous Ḥurūfī movement in 15th-century Iran testifies to the religio-cultural power of gnostic lettrism at all social levels. Ibn Turka's innovation was providing a philosophical framework that made lettrism intellectually respectable among the scholarly elite.

### Later Development and Influence

Ibn Turka's framework became canonical. By the 16th century, virtually every Islamic philosopher engaging seriously with lettrism worked through Ibn Turka's categories. The tradition continued through Safavid Iran (with thinkers like Mullā Ṣadrā), Ottoman Anatolia, and Mughal India. Lettrism remained a living intellectual tradition until the 19th century.

In modern times, the dismissal of lettrism as superstition was part of orientalist ideology. Contemporary scholarship has recognized lettrism for what it was: a legitimate intellectual system with internal coherence, grounded in rigorous reasoning, and integrated with the best scholarship of its era. It was not proto-science awaiting correction by modern physics, but rather a distinct epistemic system with different starting assumptions.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Lettrism is one of five occult sciences in Ibn Turka's classification, considered the highest because it encompasses the others.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context.* In *Islamicate Occult Sciences in Theory and Practice*, pp. 127–199.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology: Lettrism, Alchemy, and the Secrets of the Letters in Medieval Islam.* Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism.* 2023.

concepts.name: Barzakh
concepts.card: **Al-Barzakh** (the Isthmus). In Ibn Turka's system, the intermediate realm between pure matter and pure spirit, between multiplicity and unity. The domain where letters become forms, where [[divine-names]] manifest as causal powers, where mathematics governs physical existence. Central to understanding how lettrism operates—letters do not merely represent reality but constitute the barzakh through which divine principles become concrete.
concepts.body:
## Al-Barzakh: The Intermediate Realm

**Al-Barzakh** (literally, "isthmus" or "barrier") is Ibn Turka's term for the ontological middle ground between pure spirit and pure matter. Qur'anically, the barzakh refers to the barrier between the two seas that prevents them from mixing. Medieval Islamic philosophers, especially Ibn ʿArabī, adopted this to denote the intermediate realm between intellect and sense, between the divine and the created. Ibn Turka transformed this concept into the centerpiece of his metaphysical system.

In Ibn Turka's framework, the Barzakh is not merely a philosophical abstraction but the **actual location where causation operates**. The barzakh is where [[ilm-al-huruf|letters and their numerical values]] exert power. It is the realm in which:

- Divine names (*asmaʾ*) become manifest in forms (*ashkāl*)
- Letters (*hurūf*) function as operative principles
- Mathematics (abjad numerology) governs the unfolding of creation
- Intention (*niyyah*) plus ritual acts produce concrete effects

Understanding the barzakh is essential for understanding how Ibn Turka reconciles rational philosophy with operative magic. Operations that recombine letters work not through mystical intuition but through precise knowledge of how the barzakh functions as the intermediate domain where formal patterns (mathematical, linguistic, geometric) generate effects in material reality.

The barzakh is also the human soul—Ibn Turka argues that human consciousness and will operate in the barzakh, which is why knowledge of letters and divine names grants operative power. Mastery of lettrist science is mastery of the mechanisms by which barzakh-realm knowledge becomes action.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The barzakh is Ibn Turka's foundational cosmological concept; all occult operations depend on understanding it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 150-180.

concepts.name: Abjad numerology
concepts.card: **Abjad numerology** (Hisab al-Jumul). The system assigning numerical values to Arabic letters (alif=1, bāʾ=2, etc.), allowing letters and words to be manipulated mathematically. Central to [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]: Ibn Turka used abjad values to establish correspondences between divine names, cosmic principles, and human faculties. Enables the calculation of ''operative words'' whose numerical sum aligns with specific celestial or talismanic purposes.
concepts.body:
## Abjad Numerology (Hisab al-Jumul)

The **abjad system** is an ancient method of letter-to-number correspondence in Arabic and Hebrew. Each of the 28 Arabic letters carries a numerical value:
- alif (a) = 1, bāʾ (b) = 2, jīm (j) = 3... up to ghīn (gh) = 1000

This allowed Arabic letters, words, and verses to be treated as mathematical entities. The sum of a word's letters yields a number; that number can be matched against cosmic cycles, divine names, or talismanic intent.

In Ibn Turka's system, abjad numerology becomes **the bridge between language and mathematics, between expression and causation**. By selecting or composing words whose abjad sum equals a specific number—say, the number corresponding to the planet Venus or to a particular divine name—one creates a linguistic-mathematical object that resonates with that principle. Written or chanted correctly, such a word becomes operative.

Example: the divine name al-ʿAlīm ("the All-Knowing") has a specific abjad value. A talisman inscribed with a word or phrase whose abjad value matches that of al-ʿAlīm would, in theory, embody the properties of divine knowledge and could be used to attract or enhance that quality.

Ibn Turka's genius was systematizing abjad manipulation into a rigorous science rather than leaving it as scattered numerological tricks. He showed how abjad calculations, combined with proper understanding of the barzakh and divine names, provide a methodology for intentional causation grounded in cosmic principles.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Abjad is one of the core technical tools of [[ilm-al-huruf]]; mastery of it is necessary for operative lettrism.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, pp. 95-130. Ibn Turka, *Kitab al-Mafahis*, Chapters on Numerology.

concepts.name: The Divine Names
concepts.card: **Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya** (The Divine Names and Attributes). Islamic doctrine positing 28 (or 99) divine names—each expressing an aspect of God's nature (The Merciful, The Just, The Mighty, etc.). In [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], each of the 28 Arabic letters corresponds to one divine name, making letters themselves expressions of divine attributes. Ibn Turka's system treats mastery of the divine names through their corresponding letters as the path to aligning human will with cosmic principles.
concepts.body:
## The Divine Names (Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya)

Islamic theology recognizes that God is known through His attributes and names. The Qur'an references divine names, and Islamic scholars compiled lists—commonly 99, though sometimes 28. Each name expresses a dimension of divinity: al-Raḥmān (The Merciful), al-ʿAdl (The Just), al-ʿAlīm (The All-Knowing), al-Qawī (The Mighty), etc.

In [[ilm-al-huruf|Ibn Turka's lettrist system]], the 28 divine names are mapped directly onto the 28 Arabic letters. This creates a correspondence where:
- Each letter IS a divine name
- Each letter carries the properties and powers of that name
- Manipulation of letters becomes invocation of divine principles

For example:
- The letter ʿAyn corresponds to al-ʿAlīm (The All-Knowing)
- The letter Tāʾ corresponds to al-Tāʾib (The Returning/Repenting)
- The letter Qāf corresponds to al-Qawī (The Mighty)

Through understanding these correspondences and using [[abjad-numerology|abjad numerology]], a practitioner can compose words, phrases, or talismans that embody specific divine qualities. The goal is not manipulation (in the magical sense) but **attunement**: aligning human intention and action with divine attributes, thereby participating in the structure of reality itself.

Ibn Turka's treatment of the divine names through letters represents a synthesis of Islamic theology, [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist gnosis]], and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]]. It is the theological foundation that legitimizes lettrism as a valid science within Islamic orthodoxy—because engaging with letters is, from this perspective, engaging with divine attributes themselves.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The divine names are the theological anchor for [[ilm-al-huruf]]; they ground lettrist practice within Islamic doctrine.
literature: Ibn ʿArabī. *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya*, Treatise on the Divine Names.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, Ch. 3.

concepts.name: Pythagorean Cosmology
concepts.card: **Pythagorean Cosmology**. The ancient Greek doctrine that numbers and their ratios are the fundamental principles governing reality. Ibn Turka's distinctive contribution was grounding Islamic [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] explicitly in Pythagorean mathematics, arguing that letters and their [[abjad-numerology|numerical values]] encode cosmic principles just as Pythagoras taught that mathematics is the language of creation. This synthesis gave Islamic lettrism mathematical legitimacy and positioned it as a **truly universal science** encompassing reason, mysticism, and operative power.
concepts.body:
## Pythagorean Cosmology in Islamic Context

Pythagorean philosophy (c. 580–500 BCE) teaches that numbers are the fundamental constituents of reality. Numbers, through their ratios and relationships, generate harmony, order, and all manifestation. This worldview emphasizes that the cosmos is knowable through mathematics, and that mathematical knowledge grants insight into (and potentially influence over) the structure of creation.

The late-antique Neoplatonic tradition preserved and developed Pythagorean thought, eventually reaching the Islamic world through Hellenistic texts, Byzantine commentaries, and the writings of Islamic philosophers like al-Kindī and al-Fārābī. Yet lettrism in the Islamic world developed largely independently, growing from Qur'anic exegesis and gnosis without explicit Pythagorean framing.

### Ibn Turka's Innovation

Ibn Turka's genius was **explicitly connecting Islamic lettrism with Pythagorean principles**. He argued that:

1. **Letters are numbers**: Each of the 28 Arabic letters has a numerical value ([[abjad-numerology|abjad]])
2. **Numbers are cosmic**: Pythagorean mathematics describes the structure of creation
3. **Therefore, letters ARE cosmic principles**: Mastery of letters is mastery of the mathematics of creation

This move was philosophically powerful: it gave lettrism a pedigree reaching back to ancient Greece; it grounded it in mathematical reason rather than mystical intuition alone; and it positioned it as **the supreme science**, encompassing both rational (Pythagorean math) and mystical (gnostic lettrism) approaches.

By adopting the Pythagorean framework, Ibn Turka essentially reinvented lettrism as a **Neopythagorean system**—and in doing so, positioned Islamic occult philosophy as a genuine alternative universal science, rivaling and arguably exceeding the philosophical systems of contemporary Renaissance Europe.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Pythagorean cosmology is Ibn Turka's foundational theoretical framework; it structures his entire philosophical system.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography*.

concepts.name: The Imaginal Realm
concepts.literal_meaning: The realm of forms; the world of imagination
concepts.card: **Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl** (The Imaginal Realm). In [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysics, the ontological layer between pure intellect and material sense where forms (*ashkāl*) exist independently of physical matter. The domain where mystical visions occur, where symbols manifest, where divine names express themselves in subtle forms. Central to understanding how knowledge operates in Islamic mysticism and occultism: the imaginal realm is where letters and divine names acquire form, where talismanic operations work, where the barzakh functions.
concepts.body:
## Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl: The Imaginal Realm

**Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl** (literally "the imaginal realm" or "the realm of imagination") is [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] term for an intermediate ontological domain between pure intellect (ʿaql) and material sensation (ḥiss). The Arabic word *khiyāl* is often mistranslated as "imagination" in the modern sense (the faculty of fantasy); Ibn Arabi means something far more precise and metaphysically serious: a realm of subtle forms (*ashkāl*) that possess reality independent of physical matter.

The imaginal realm occupies the same position in Ibn Arabi's cosmology that the [[barzakh|barzakh]] occupies in Ibn Turka's refinement of it: the crucial intermediate domain where causation operates, where divine principles become manifest in form, where knowledge acquires structure.

### Three Realms of Being

Ibn Arabi divides creation into three principal domains:

1. **The Intelligible Realm** (*ʿālam al-ʿaql*): Pure intellect, transcendent principles, divine names in their unmanifested essence
2. **The Imaginal Realm** (*ʿālam al-khiyāl*): Forms, symbols, subtle bodies, the world of vision and mystical knowledge
3. **The Sensible Realm** (*ʿālam al-ḥiss*): Material existence, the physical world knowable through sense perception

Each realm participates in the others; none is hermetically sealed. The imaginal realm serves as the *medium* through which the intelligible becomes sensible, through which the transcendent becomes immanent.

### The Imaginal in Mystical Experience

For Ibn Arabi, mystical visions (*mushāhadāt*) are not hallucinations or mere psychological phenomena—they are direct perception of the imaginal realm. When a mystic "sees" an angel, perceives a divine light, or encounters a teacher in a dream, they are perceiving realities that exist in the imaginal realm. These perceptions are as real as sensory experience, though they operate in a different ontological register.

This doctrine revolutionizes Islamic mysticism: it legitimizes mystical experience as a form of genuine knowledge by establishing that there is an objective realm (the imaginal) in which such experiences occur. Mysticism is not projection; it is perception.

### The Imaginal in Occult Practice

[[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] and the later occult philosophers adopted this framework. When a practitioner creates a talisman by writing letters and numbers with specific intention, the operation works in the imaginal realm first: the talisman, as an imaginal object (a form constituted by [[abjad-numerology|numerical correspondences]] and divine names), exerts influence on the sensible world. The imaginal realm is where the power resides; the physical talisman is the expression.

Similarly, [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist operations]] work because letters—as forms carrying [[divine-names|divine names]]—are primarily imaginal realities. Mastery of letters grants access to the imaginal realm, whence all material creation flows.

### Legacy and Transmission

[[qunavi|Qūnavī]] elaborated Ibn Arabi's doctrine of the imaginal realm into a full philosophy of knowledge (*gnosis* vs. *reason*). Through the [[qunavi|Qūnavī]]-Jandī school, the imaginal realm became part of the theoretical apparatus available to philosophers, mystics, and occultists across the Islamic world. By Ibn Turka's time, the imaginal realm was accepted as a foundational concept: its reality was presupposed, not debated.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The imaginal realm is Ibn Arabi's key metaphysical contribution; all later Islamic occultism presupposes it.
literature: Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Imaginal Ontology and the New Brethren of Purity*.

concepts.name: Talismanic Science
concepts.card: **ilm al-Talasim** (Talismanic Science). Operative practice of creating talismans inscribed with letters, numbers, divine names. Based on theory that letters, numerical correspondences, and divine names are cosmic principles that, combined correctly with proper intention, exert force through intermediate realm. Central practical application of Ibn Turka's system.
concepts.body: **Talismanic science** (ilm al-talasim) is the operative discipline of creating objects—rings, seals, parchments, metals—inscribed with carefully chosen letters, numbers, and divine names to accomplish specific aims. Unlike superstition, talismanic science in Ibn Turka's systematization is grounded in rigorous cosmological theory. A talisman works: (1) Each 28 Arabic letter corresponds to divine name and cosmic power. (2) Combining letters by numerical correspondence (*abjad*) aligns word with specific principle (Venus, al-Alim, etc.). (3) Inscribing this word-object on appropriate matter with proper intention embodies the principle. (4) Through intermediate realm, talismanic object exerts influence—attracting love, granting wisdom, protecting. Creating talisman requires: knowledge of letter values and divine correspondences, understanding of cosmic geometry and celestial timing, appropriate mental state, correct materials, proper ritual. In Ibn Turka's framework, talismanic science is not magic compelling spirits but sophisticated technology of imaginal realm. Talismans work because they express cosmic principles; they align practitioner's will with creation's structure. This gives talismanic practice philosophical and theological legitimacy: not sorcery but gnosis applied to practice.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Talismanic science is primary practical expression of lettrism; demonstrates operative efficacy.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court, Ch. 4.

concepts.name: Peripatetic Philosophy
concepts.literal_meaning: Philosophy of those who walk (Aristotelian school)
concepts.card: **Al-Falsafa al-Mashaʾiya** (Peripatetic Philosophy). The Aristotelian philosophical tradition as transmitted and developed in Islamic world. Emphasizes rational inquiry, logical syllogism, study of natural world, metaphysics grounded in being and causation. Ibn Turka synthesized peripatetic logic and metaphysics with [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], arguing that occult science achieves what peripatetic philosophy merely attempts—systematic knowledge of causation and being.
concepts.body: **Peripatetic philosophy** (*al-falsafa al-mashaʾiya*) refers to the Aristotelian tradition as developed and transmitted in the Islamic world. The name derives from Aristotle's practice of teaching while walking (*peripateo*) in the Lyceum. Islamic philosophers—al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina—adopted and adapted Aristotelian logic, metaphysics, and natural philosophy, integrating them with Islamic theology and the philosophical heritage of Greek Neoplatonism. Key commitments: (1) Reason (*ʿaql*) is primary tool for understanding reality. (2) Logic (syllogistic reasoning) provides rigorous methodology. (3) Being (*wujud*) is fundamental category; understanding causation requires understanding gradations and dependencies of being. (4) Metaphysics is possible: systematic knowledge of principles transcending particular things. By Ibn Turka's era, peripatetic philosophy was the dominant intellectual framework across Islamic world. But Ibn Turka and his circle saw its limitations: peripatetic method, while rigorous, remained abstract and speculative. It described cosmic structure but did not engage it operatively. Peripatetic philosophers asked *how* creation unfolds; Ibn Turka asked *how to participate in its unfolding*. By integrating peripatetic logic with [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], Ibn Turka claimed to achieve what peripatetic philosophy merely attempted—systematic, rationally grounded knowledge of causation and being that is simultaneously operative (producing real effects). In this sense, Ibn Turka's system transcends peripatetic philosophy by incorporating and surpassing it.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Peripatetic philosophy is the dominant rational framework Ibn Turka synthesizes with and transcends through lettrism.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Powers of One, pp. 100-140.

concepts.name: Sufism
concepts.card: **Al-Tasawwuf** (Sufism). Islamic mysticism emphasizing direct experiential knowledge of the divine through discipline, contemplation, and often ecstatic experience. Developed systematically from 9th century onward; by Ibn Turka's era, Sufism was integral to Islamic orthodoxy. [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi]], [[suhrawardi|Suhrawardi]], [[al-ghazali|Al-Ghazali]], and other philosophical predecessors were Sufi-philosophers. Ibn Turka inherited and operationalized Sufi gnosis through lettrism, positioning occult science as Sufi practice systematized into rational discipline.
concepts.body:
## Sufism: Islamic Mysticism and Spiritual Practice

**Al-Tasawwuf** (Sufism) is Islamic mysticism—the disciplined pursuit of direct experiential knowledge (*dhawq*; literally "tasting") of divine reality. Sufism emerged in the 8th-9th centuries as ascetic movement emphasizing renunciation, devotion, and intimate knowledge of God. By the medieval period, it had become systematized into orders (*tariqas*) with formal training, ritual practices, and hierarchical initiation. Key Sufi commitments: (1) Reason alone cannot reach ultimate truth; direct mystical intuition is necessary. (2) The soul possesses faculties beyond intellect—faculties for perceiving divine light and truth. (3) Ascetic discipline, remembrance (*dhikr*), and sincere devotion purify the soul and grant illumination. (4) The spiritual master (*shaykh*) guides disciples on the path. By Ibn Turka's era, Sufism was thoroughly integrated into Islamic orthodoxy. Major philosophical-theologians—[[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi]], [[suhrawardi|Suhrawardi]], [[al-ghazali|Al-Ghazali]]—were simultaneously Sufi mystics and systematic philosophers. Sufism provided the conceptual vocabulary and experiential framework for occult philosophy: if the soul can experience divine light directly, if mystical knowledge is genuine, then the soul's interaction with the imaginal realm and its deployment of lettrist gnosis are not irrational but expressions of mystical capacity. Ibn Turka inherited Sufi gnosis and transformed it: where Sufi masters cultivated mystical states through meditation and discipline, Ibn Turka systematized the underlying principles and made them operative through lettrist-talismanic technique. Sufi mysticism became Sufi science.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Sufism is the experiential-spiritual foundation upon which Ibn Turka builds his rational occult science; all mystical vocabulary derives from Sufi tradition.
literature: Chittick, William C. The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination.

concepts.name: Occult Science as Universal System
concepts.card: **Occult Science as Universal System**. The core historiographical claim that Ibn Turka and the Isfahan Circle systematized Islamic lettrism, talismanism, and numerology into a comprehensive philosophy claiming universal validity—a science encompassing metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, cosmology, and operative practice. Not marginal superstition but legitimate intellectual achievement rivaling any philosophical school. Melvin-Koushki's central argument.
concepts.body: The claim that Islamic occultism constitutes a genuine universal science—this is the animating thesis of Melvin-Koushki's entire body of work and the central historiographical claim of Ibn Turka's own project. What did occultism offer that rational philosophy did not? (1) Integration of knowledge and practice: peripatetic philosophy described the cosmos; occult science engaged it operatively. (2) Rigor grounded in systematic principle: not folk magic or superstition but coherent system derived from fundamental doctrines (divine names, letters, Pythagorean numbers). (3) Universality: not provincial tradition but claim to encompass all knowledge—metaphysics via cosmology, epistemology via gnosis, ethics via attunement to cosmic principles. (4) Legitimacy within orthodoxy: by grounding lettrist science in Ibn Arabi's metaphysics and Pythagorean philosophy, Ibn Turka positioned it not as heresy but as sophisticated development within Islamic orthodoxy. The claim to universality is not arrogance but serious metaphysical commitment: if letters are cosmic principles and divine names are ontological foundations, then knowledge of letters and names is knowledge of reality itself—hence universal. This positioning of occult science as universal system represents a major historiographical revaluation: instead of viewing Islamic philosophy as decline into mysticism and formalism, we see a tradition of genuine innovation and intellectual achievement.
concepts.hierarchy_note: This historiographical frame unites all entries; it is the meta-argument justifying the entire project.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography.

concepts.name: Neoplatonism
concepts.card: **Neoplatonism**. The late-antique emanationist philosophy of Plotinus and Proclus, which reached Islamdom in Arabic translation and was never, in Melvin-Koushki's usage, quite separable from its Pythagorean twin — he writes of *neopythagorean-neoplatonic* philosophy as one tradition. Ibn Turka's contribution was not to receive it but to **reclassify** it: he treated this philosophy as prophetically revealed rather than merely Greek, and made its mathematics the ground on which the occult sciences could be defended as sciences at all.
concepts.body:
## Neoplatonism, and what Ibn Turka did to it
